candidates.title: Every AI Agent Action Needs a Receipt
candidates.author: Future AGI
candidates.reason: The reader asks a concrete architecture question about preventing an independent verifier from becoming a single point of trust.
candidates.evidence: The response distinguishes timeout ambiguity from failure, identifies double-application risk during retries, and asks how the verifier itself should be governed.
candidates.draftResponse: That is the right failure mode to challenge. I would avoid a singular verifier and use a tiered verification quorum: an authoritative system-of-record read, a policy-specific postcondition check, and an independently operated evaluator for high-impact actions. The receipt should preserve each verifier's identity, evidence digest, result, disagreement, and timeout; unresolved disagreement fails closed or escalates. Shadow cases, canaries, and fault injection then test the verification layer itself, so trust rests on diverse evidence and visible disagreement rather than one component.

candidates.title: Adobe Summit Mumbai 2026: measurable experience consistency
candidates.author: Manisha chouhan
candidates.reason: This is a direct, substantive reply to the user's existing comment and should be handled before outbound engagement.
candidates.evidence: Manisha agreed that reliable processes create a seamless customer experience and specifically highlighted consistency as measurable.
candidates.draftResponse: Agreed, @Manisha chouhan. The useful operating measures are the percentage of event failures absorbed without attendee impact, handoff variance, and recovery time. If those improve while satisfaction stays high, the experience is not only seamless; the operating model is resilient.

candidates.title: Should agents appear on the org chart?
candidates.author: Pascal BORNET
candidates.reason: The post opens a high-quality discussion about agent ownership, accountability, and organizational design that closely matches the user's control-plane positioning.
candidates.evidence: Pascal contrasts direct-report, agent-pod, and shared-infrastructure models and argues that an org chart can make hidden agent work and human ownership visible.
candidates.draftResponse: Putting agents on the org chart helps ownership, but I would add an authority chart beside it. @Pascal BORNET, four fields should travel with every agent: named human principal, maximum delegated scope, approval threshold, and kill-switch owner. Otherwise visible accountability can still hide who spent whose authority.

candidates.title: AI employees should preserve human agency
candidates.author: Cael Stewart
candidates.reason: The post directly challenges fully autonomous agent designs and has an active, relevant discussion with 30 reactions and 20 comments.
candidates.evidence: Cael notes that 10–20 well-funded startups are pursuing AI employees and argues that winners will keep critical decisions human while automating execution.
candidates.draftResponse: The 10–20 funded entrants make the control boundary more important, not less. @Cael Stewart, I would measure human-agency preservation through escalation precision, unauthorized-action rate, verified completion rate, and recovery time. A winner should maximize successful execution without silently converting ambiguity into autonomy.

candidates.title: The AI Control Plane: Building Trust, Governance, and Accountability
candidates.author: Farrukh Ahmed Khan
candidates.reason: The article covers runtime policy, identity, observability, FinOps, MCP, A2A, and human oversight—the core architecture themes in the user's catalog.
candidates.evidence: Farrukh compares the emerging agent control plane with the role API gateways played in the API economy and asks how enterprises are governing agents at scale.
candidates.draftResponse: The API-gateway analogy is strong, but an agent control plane must govern intent and effect, not only traffic. @Farrukh Ahmed Khan, I would make five runtime measures non-negotiable: policy-decision latency, unauthorized-action rate, evidence completeness, postcondition-verification success, and mean recovery time.

candidates.title: Who controls the agent?
candidates.author: Vikram V. Koppikar
candidates.reason: The article asks who is accountable by name for harmful agent actions and supplies seven concrete pre-deployment governance questions.
candidates.evidence: Vikram asks who approved the agent, what data and prohibitions apply, where humans intervene, who contains failure, who monitors it, and who is personally accountable.
candidates.draftResponse: Naming accountability is necessary, but the seven answers should also become machine-verifiable control data. @Vikram V. Koppikar, bind each action to its principal, policy version, scoped permission, approval evidence, outcome verifier, and recovery owner; then measure orphaned actions and exception-closure time.

candidates.title: Your AI coding agent sees files. Not the system.
candidates.author: Anuj J.
candidates.reason: The post provides benchmark evidence that knowledge-graph context can improve coding-agent quality and search efficiency while lowering run cost.
candidates.evidence: GitNexus reports 68.4% solved versus 37.0% without graph context, 51% lower cost per run, and 45k+ GitHub stars.
candidates.draftResponse: @Akon Labs (YC S26), moving from 37.0% to 68.4% solved while cutting run cost 51% suggests graph context affects both quality and search efficiency. The enterprise test I would add is blast-radius precision: how many predicted dependencies were real, and how many critical callers were missed?

candidates.title: LLM Memory Architecture
candidates.author: Sanjay Kumar Ph.D., MBA
candidates.reason: The post frames production LLM memory as a three-tier architecture and explicitly discusses latency, recall, persistence, privacy, cost, and controlled forgetting.
candidates.evidence: The source describes working, episodic, and semantic memory tiers plus routing, consolidation, privacy controls, and deletion trade-offs.
candidates.draftResponse: @Sanjay Kumar, the three-tier model becomes operational only when each tier has an explicit retention and deletion contract. I would track recall at k, stale-fact rate, p95 retrieval latency, privacy-deletion SLA, and the percentage of answers whose memory provenance can be reconstructed.

candidates.title: Flexible billing and cost controls for Gemini Enterprise
candidates.author: Thomas Kurian
candidates.reason: The post introduces four concrete AI cost controls, including spend caps, savings commitments, and automatic model routing.
candidates.evidence: The source describes four controls and up to 20% token-cost savings; current revalidation showed 802 reactions, 33 comments, and 63 reposts.
candidates.draftResponse: @Thomas Kurian, the 20% token-saving commitment is useful, but the stronger control is tying spend caps to outcome SLOs. Teams should see cost per verified task, fallback rate, model-route distribution, and quality-adjusted savings; otherwise auto-routing can look cheaper while shifting cost into rework.

candidates.title: Context engineering starts with one decision
candidates.author: Manas Jain
candidates.reason: The post proposes a decision-first build order for enterprise agents and makes permissions and trusted context explicit before tools and actions.
candidates.evidence: The source sequence is Decision → Required Context → Trusted Sources → Permissions → Tools → Action and includes ten diagnostic context questions.
candidates.draftResponse: @Manas Jain, Decision → Context → Sources → Permissions → Tools → Action is the right build order. I would add Verification → Recovery, then instrument p95 decision latency, approval rate, false-escalation rate, successful postcondition checks, and mean time to reverse an incorrect action.

candidates.title: AWS welcomes DuckLabs
candidates.author: Swami Sivasubramanian
candidates.reason: The acquisition discussion is directly relevant to enterprise analytics architecture, operational weight, data movement, and governed production deployment.
candidates.evidence: The source welcomes DuckLabs to AWS and frames the opportunity as making analytics faster, simpler, and more cost-effective; current revalidation showed 937 reactions, 17 comments, and 36 reposts.
candidates.draftResponse: @Swami Sivasubramanian, DuckDB's appeal is moving analytics to the data with very little operational weight. The acquisition opportunity for AWS is measurable: query latency, cross-service data movement, price-performance, and time from local prototype to governed production should improve without weakening workload portability.

candidates.title: Secure Agent Authorization — How It Works
candidates.author: Eric Broda
candidates.reason: Directly extends the article’s eight-step scoped-grant architecture with replay resistance, effect bounds, signed outcome receipts, and business-state verification.
candidates.evidence: Full free 2-minute article read in the signed-in Medium UI. It defines eight stages from orchestrated request through trust-authority registry checks, a task/tool/skill/expiry/evidence-bound execution grant, executor validation, and recorded tool outcome. No existing response from this profile was visible. Score: relevance 0.98, discussion quality 0.55, unique contribution 0.94, recency 0.50; weighted 0.77.
candidates.draftResponse: Eric, the eight-step chain puts the trust boundary in the right place: the executor, not the model, enforces scope. I would make the grant single-use—or explicitly count-bounded—and bind it to an action hash, resource, maximum side effect, and post-condition. Expiry alone does not prevent replay inside the validity window. The executor should return a signed outcome receipt, and the verifier should compare the observed business state with the requested state, not merely accept a successful tool response.

candidates.title: A Skills-Based Pattern for AI Agents in Microsoft Foundry
candidates.author: Velmurugan Muthaiyan
candidates.reason: Adds the missing governance contract for reusable skills and connects version resolution to execution receipts and bounded authority.
candidates.evidence: Full post and visible discussion read in the signed-in LinkedIn UI: the post separates agent, skill, tool, and toolbox and reports 34 reactions, 2 comments, and 3 reposts after two days. No existing comment by this profile was visible. Score: relevance 0.96, discussion quality 0.58, unique contribution 0.93, recency 0.90; weighted 0.85.
candidates.draftResponse: @Velmurugan Muthaiyan, the separation is valuable, but the governance boundary needs to attach to each versioned skill and tool contract—not only to the agent. I would make every skill declare its input/output schema, data classification, permitted tools, maximum authority, confirmation rule, idempotency behavior, and compensation path. Pin that skill version in the execution receipt; otherwise a stable agent can change behavior silently when the toolbox resolves a newer skill.

candidates.title: It is always 17: LLMs and random-number selection
candidates.author: Maria Sukhareva
candidates.reason: Converts the observed 17-selection bias into a measurable sampling test and a production control for entropy-sensitive tasks.
candidates.evidence: Full post and visible discussion read in the signed-in LinkedIn UI: three independent prompts per model mostly returned 17; the post had 127 reactions, 38 comments, and 7 reposts after one day. No existing comment by this profile was visible. Score: relevance 0.78, discussion quality 0.94, unique contribution 0.92, recency 0.95; weighted 0.88.
candidates.draftResponse: @Maria Sukhareva, this is useful precisely because “pick” is not “sample.” For three draws per model, the result is diagnostic, not yet inferential; I’d repeat 1,000+ independent calls and test the observed distribution against uniformity. In production, entropy-sensitive tasks should route to a cryptographic PRNG/tool and record the tool identity, sample space, and acceptance test. Natural-language competence is not evidence of statistical randomness.

candidates.title: Prisma AIRS and executive authorization metrics
candidates.author: Dhari A.
candidates.reason: Directly answers an inbound technical response by translating blocked actions and recovery into executive-grade risk and control metrics.
candidates.evidence: Dhari replied to the existing governance comment that Palo Alto Networks Idira addresses agent identity and authorization, and identified blocked high-impact actions and successful recovery as the strongest executive metrics. The source post had 253 reactions and 24 comments; the reply was 19 minutes old when inspected. Score: relevance 0.98, discussion quality 0.88, unique contribution 0.88, recency 0.99; weighted 0.94.
candidates.draftResponse: @Dhari A., agreed. Idira makes the authorization layer concrete; the next executive step is to connect each blocked action to avoided loss and each recovery to restoration time. I would report blocked high-impact actions by policy reason, false-block rate, mean time to revoke, verified recovery rate, and residual exposure after recovery. That separates controls that merely stop activity from controls that measurably reduce business risk.
